title: Results in the 2026 Alaska State Senate and House elections - FairVote

Results in the 2026 Alaska State Senate and House elections - FairVote 
 Results in the 2026 Alaska State Senate and House elections
 Bryan Huang 
  | 
 November 19, 2026 
 Share 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 Linkedin 
 Email 
 All votes have been counted in Alaska’s critical ranked choice voting (RCV) elections for Congress, governor, and State Legislature . Every seat in the Alaska House of Representatives was up for election, along with half of the seats in the State Senate.
 This election saw Alaska’s highest midterm turnout ever. Since election day, cross-partisan majority coalitions have formed to lead both houses of the State Legislature ; this has happened in all three election cycles since Alaska implemented RCV and open primaries. 
 Republicans, Democrats, and independents will all serve in leadership roles – including Republicans as Senate president and majority leader , an independent as House speaker , and a Democrat as Senate rules chair . These leaders will make policy alongside newly elected Democratic Governor Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.
 14 state legislative races were decided by ranked choice voting tallies, since no candidate won a majority of voters’ first choices. Those races were: Senate Districts C, M, O and S, and House Districts 23, 24, 25, 28, 29, 30, 33, 37, 38 and 39. 
 In these contests, RCV delivered majority winners in multi-candidate fields, and allowed voters to express their full range of preferences without fear of “wasting” their vote. Across these contests, 13% more votes counted meaningfully because of RCV – representing voters whose first choice was eliminated, but who still had their ballot count for one of the two finalist candidates. 
 Overall, Alaska’s election system fosters greater voter choice and more competition in general elections. Read on for highlights from the 2026 Alaska State Senate and House elections. FairVote analyzed Alaska’s statewide elections in a separate post .
 A record year for independent candidates
 Eight independents were elected to the Alaska State Legislature this year, including seven in the House and one in the Senate. That’s a record number of independent legislators in the Last Frontier. 
 One notable race was in State Senate District S, where two independents, one Republican, and one Democrat ran for an open seat. Independent Bryce Edgmon won with 58% of votes, after leading with 36% of voters’ first choices. Edgmon won partly because he was a popular backup choice for supporters of Democrat Wassilie Guy: In the RCV tally, Guy’s supporters preferred Edgmon over Republican Darren Morgan Deacon by a nearly 2-to-1 margin.
 Edgmon currently serves as speaker of the Alaska State House – and is the first Alaska Native to hold that position. He has already been chosen to serve in the State Senate majority coalition’s leadership as one of two finance chairs .
 A “come-from-behind” win in State Senate District M
 Three Republicans and one Democrat ran in State Senate District M. Republican incumbent Cathy Tilton received 33% of first choices, followed by Republican challenger Ryan Berry with 32%.
 Voters who supported the third- and fourth-place candidates, Democrat Patricia Chesbro and Republican Zane Vrvilo, supported Berry as their next choice by nearly a 2-to-1 margin, helping Berry surpass Tilton in the RCV count. 
 There are also possible “come-from-behind” wins in House Districts 29 and 30, but these races are close enough that they may proceed to a recount. Read more in the “Close races and possible recounts” section. 
It’s rare for a candidate to “come from behind” in an RCV race – but it’s a feature of the system, not a bug. In single-winner RCV races since 2004, the candidate with the most first-choice support has won 94% of the time. Candidates win an RCV election by building both deep (1st-choice) and broad (backup choice) support. 
 Come-from-behind victories usually occur when a polarizing candidate struggles to win backup-choice support – and/or when the majority splits its first-choice support among similar candidates, and then consolidates their vote behind the strongest of those candidates. In this case, a late scandal involving the longtime incumbent Tilton may have discouraged voters outside her base from ranking her as a backup choice. 
 Close races and possible recounts
 Several House districts were decided by extremely narrow margins, and may go to recounts. 
 Alaska House elections have gone to recounts before, including prior to the adoption of RCV. In 2018, a tied race in Alaska House District 1 went to a recount; Republican Bart LeBon won by one vote. Since Alaska adopted RCV in 2022, there have been three state legislative recounts. From 2018 to 2024, the largest shift in margin in an Alaska State House general election recount was three votes.
 In House District 29, incumbent Republican Garret Nelson and challenger Republican Steve Menard are neck-and-neck in first choices, with 34.0% and 33.5%, respectively. Voters who ranked Democrat Kimberly Slone or independent candidate Jessica Kusner-Kalarchik first slightly preferred Menard over Nelson – but not enough for Menard to overtake Nelson in the RCV tally. Nelson is ahead by four votes.
 House District 30 saw a three-way race between incumbent Republican Kevin McCabe, Republican Doug Massie, and Democrat Sandra Loomis. Kevin McCabe is part of the Republican minority caucus in the State House, which Doug Massie also said he’d join if elected. 
 McCabe received 37% of first choices, followed by Massie with 33% and Loomis with 30%. Voters who ranked Loomis first preferred Massie to McCabe by more than a 2-to-1 margin, helping Massie overtake McCabe in the RCV tally by three votes. 
 Given the incredibly close margins in Districts 29 and 30, recounts could change the result of either race. Regardless of who wins, the winners will have a majority of votes and a clear mandate to lead with RCV. 
 Alaskans vote to keep ranked choice voting
 Alaskans also voted on whether to keep ranked choice voting for future elections. The full reform package at stake included RCV, Alaska’s top four primary, and an anti-dark money rule requiring the public disclosure of contributions over $2,000.
 “No” on repeal won 54-46% – the largest margin in all three of Alaska’s votes on its election system, and a larger margin than any statewide candidate for office this year. 
 In a 2024 survey, 84% of Alaska voters said ranked choice voting is simple. Since Alaska adopted its election reforms, the state’s elections have become more competitive .
 Why did the final results take 15 days?
 Alaska accepts absentee ballots up to 15 days after the election, and the state has a long history of extended vote-counting that predates its adoption of ranked choice voting. Many ballots arrive late in Alaska’s 15 day window because of the state’s size; tens of thousands of voters live in areas reachable only by boat or plane.
 In two recent close U.S. Senate races, the winner was declared at the end of the 15-day period – Sen. Lisa Murkowski in 2010, and Mark Begich in 2008. More recently, in 2024, Ballot Measure 2 – a “Yes/No” vote regarding Alaska’s election system – also took all 15 days.
 The RCV tally itself is just the click of a button and nearly instantaneous. Yesterday, an Alaska Division of Elections official tabulated the official RCV results for 15 races in just 24 minutes – during this time, he also explained the round-by-round results of each contest in detail. Though the Division of Elections conducted its official RCV tallies yesterday, the results of most races have been clear for some time. RCV results can be analyzed and projected ahead of final tallies, just like any other election results. 
 Starting election night, the Alaska Division of Elections released a preliminary cast vote record (CVR) – an anonymized digital record of ballots – allowing analysts to run unofficial RCV tallies of the ballots counted so far. The Division released updated CVRs as more ballots were counted, in the same way other states release updated vote totals over time.
 FairVote produced preliminary RCV tallies for the statewide races as the cast vote records were updated, and also created an interactive tool showing who was on track to win and how results could change as remaining votes were counted. FairVote’s preliminary RCV tallies were nearly identical to the official tallies released on November 18, and could be used to project election outcomes. Several news outlets published their own analyses, with the New York Times reporting on November 5 that Democrat Mary Peltola was “on track to eventually prevail in the Alaska Senate race.”
 We appreciate the Alaska Division of Elections’ decision to release preliminary cast vote record data, which is also available for state legislative races. This increases transparency, and offers a reminder that RCV results can be produced as quickly as those in non-RCV elections.
